summary: Lists the information that must be provisioned on a customer edge router for several transition methods that carry IPv4 over IPv6 using tunnels. It aims to define reusable components, and to the extent provisioning is dynamic, to carry them in AAA attributes.

eli5.summary: When a home router needs setup details for sending old-style traffic over the new network, this lists them.

questions: how to provision ipv4-over-ipv6 on a cpe
what radius attributes support dslite and map
what diameter avps support ds-lite and map-e
what is a port set identifier
subtitle: Diameter attributes that carry the per-subscriber settings a home router needs for DS-Lite, lw4o6 and MAP-E.

tldr.problem: Operators moving to IPv6 use several methods to carry IPv4 over IPv6, and each needs subscriber-specific settings on the customer router that AAA servers have no standard way to deliver.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes what DS-Lite, lw4o6 and MAP-E need, then defines 16 Diameter AVPs (codes 632 to 647) that reuse common pieces such as the border router name and multicast prefixes.
tldr.outcome: AAA can hand a provisioning node everything needed to configure the customer equipment, with the Grouped AVP present indicating which method the subscriber uses.

today: RFC 7678 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of these Diameter AVPs.

sections.title: The Provisioning Problem
sections.content:
Several transition techniques let IPv4 packets cross an IPv6 network while using as few public IPv4 addresses as possible. Different operators deploy different ones, and one operator may use more than one. Each technique needs some subscriber-specific information on the customer edge device (CPE, Customer Premise Equipment).

The RFC does not care how that information finally reaches the CPE (DHCPv6 or something else). It assumes the data is managed by AAA servers and handed to intermediate nodes using Diameter (RFC 6733). It covers Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333), Lightweight 4over6 (RFC 7596) and MAP-E (RFC 7597), plus multicast for all three.

No new Diameter commands or Application IDs are specified. The AVPs can be used by any Diameter application suitable for provisioning.
sections.eli5: A home router has to be told a few facts before it can use a new kind of road. This document is the checklist of facts, plus the labels for sending them.

sections.title: What Each Transition Method Needs
sections.content:
DS-Lite. The B4 element needs the address of the AFTR (border router). The AAA server supplies the AFTR's FQDN. The B4 tunnel interface address (192.0.0.2 to 192.0.0.7, default 192.0.0.2) is assumed to be set by other means, because several B4 instances may share a device.

lw4o6. Four items: the border router's IPv6 address, an IPv6 prefix used to build the tunnel source address (the Binding Prefix), the IPv4 address for the external side, and, if that address is shared, the port set. The border router needs the same IPv4 and port data bound to the full /128 tunnel source address, so the two configurations must be kept in sync.

MAP-E. The CPE needs the border relay addresses, its end-user IPv6 prefix, a Basic Mapping Rule (rule IPv6 prefix and length, rule IPv4 prefix and length, number of EA bits, port set parameters), whether to use Mesh or Hub-and-Spoke mode, and in Mesh mode zero or more Forwarding Mapping Rules. Configuring the border router is out of scope.

Multicast. Three prefixes: ASM-mPrefix64, SSM-mPrefix64 and uPrefix64, used to build IPv4-embedded IPv6 multicast addresses.
sections.eli5: Each way of sending old traffic over the new network needs its own short shopping list: where the gateway is, which address and which slice of ports you may use.

sections.title: Port Sets and Choosing a Method
sections.content:
When an external IPv4 address is shared, lw4o6 and MAP-E restrict the CPE to a subset of ports. Both use the algorithm in Appendix B of RFC 7597, with three parameters: an offset a from the start of the port number to the first bit of the PSID (Port Set Identifier), the PSID length k in bits, and the PSID value itself. The default for a is 0 for lw4o6 and 6 for MAP-E.

The RFC picks the method by which Grouped AVP is sent. AAA passes only the Grouped AVP for lw4o6 or for MAP-E, so the operator controls the choice. No Grouped AVP and only the AFTR's FQDN present means DS-Lite. Multicast provisioning is independent of the method.
sections.eli5: If many houses share one phone number, each house gets certain extension numbers. The port set says which extensions your router may use.

sections.title: The Attribute-Value Pairs
sections.content:
The AVPs use codes 632 to 647. Shared building blocks:

  • IP-Prefix-Length (632): length of an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, 0 to 32 or 0 to 128, with tighter limits in some contexts.
  • Border-Router-Name (633): an FQDN as an OctetString, following RFC 1035, RFC 1123 and RFC 2181, in ASCII (A-labels for IDNs).
  • Port-Set-Identifier (639): four octets (Offset 0 to 15, PSIDLength 0 to 16 minus a, and a two-octet PSIDValue right justified). A PSIDLength of 0 means the value is ignored.

For multicast, 64-Multicast-Attributes (634) groups ASM-mPrefix64 (635), SSM-mPrefix64 (636) and a Delegated-IPv6-Prefix used as uPrefix64. It MUST include the ASM or SSM prefix and MAY include both. The Delegated-IPv6-Prefix MUST be present when the SSM prefix is. ASM prefix lengths are 24 to 96.

For lw4o6, Lw4o6-Binding (640) groups Tunnel-Source-Pref-Or-Addr (637), which holds either a Delegated-IPv6-Prefix or a Tunnel-Source-IPv6-Address (638) but not both, plus Lw4o6-External-IPv4-Addr (641) and an optional Port-Set-Identifier.

For MAP-E, MAP-E-Attributes (642) groups one or more Border-Router-Name and MAP-Mapping-Rule AVPs, an optional MAP-Mesh-Mode (643, 0 = MESH, 1 = HUB_AND_SPOKE) and an optional Delegated-IPv6-Prefix. Without the mesh indicator the CPE uses Hub-and-Spoke mode, where extra mapping rules MUST NOT be present. MAP-Mapping-Rule (644) requires Rule-IPv4-Addr-Or-Prefix (645), Rule-IPv6-Prefix (646), EA-Field-Length (647, 0 to 48) and a Port-Set-Identifier.
sections.eli5: Each setting gets a numbered label, like a form with boxes. Some boxes hold other boxes, so one message can carry a whole set of settings.

sections.title: Flags and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Section 4 gives the AVP flag rules: for every AVP defined here the V bit MUST NOT be set. The M-bit usage for an AVP in a command may be defined by the application, as in the Diameter base protocol.

IANA has registered the 16 codes 632 to 647 in the Diameter "AVP Codes" registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of label numbers now has these sixteen new labels, so no one else can use the same numbers.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Both threats involve man-in-the-middle attacks on the Diameter delivery path. Altered AVP contents could cause denial of service through misconfiguration (for example an invalid IP address), or let a misbehaving node intercept traffic if a fake border node is configured. Also, Diameter security is hop-by-hop, and the RFC notes that at the time of writing the end-to-end problem was not solved, so Diameter peers along the path could mount attacks.

The AVPs reveal subscriber addresses that can be used for tracking, so they are all considered security sensitive. The considerations in Section 13.3 of RFC 6733 MUST be followed for messages containing them.
sections.eli5: Someone sitting in the middle could change the settings and break your connection or send you to a fake gateway. The settings also show addresses, so they must be kept private.

fields.name: Offset
fields.desc: Offset a from the start of the port number to the PSID; valid values 0 to 15.

fields.name: PSIDLength
fields.desc: Length k of the PSID in bits; 0 means no PSID and the value is ignored.

fields.name: PSIDValue
fields.desc: The PSID, right justified in the field.
